title: Backtracking
description:
```cpp
std::vector<std::vector<int>> combinationsSumming(std::vector<int> numbers, int target);   // each number at most once
std::vector<std::vector<int>> uniquePermutations(std::vector<int> numbers);                 // no duplicates, lexicographic order
long long countQueens(int n);
bool solveSudoku(std::vector<std::string>& board);                                          // 9 strings of 9 chars, '.' for empty
```

- `combinationsSumming`: the numbers are positive and distinct. Return every subset that sums to `target`, each sorted ascending, and the list sorted lexicographically. Prune: stop extending a combination once its sum would pass the target (sort the numbers first).
- `uniquePermutations`: the input may contain duplicates; return each distinct ordering once, in lexicographic order, without using a set to remove duplicates. (Sort first, and at each position skip a value equal to the previous one that is not in use.)
- `countQueens`: the number of ways to place n non-attacking queens on an n × n board, with O(1) safety checks. The tests go up to n = 12.
- `solveSudoku` fills the board in place and returns true, or returns false (leaving the board as it was) if there is no solution. Choose the empty cell with the fewest candidates first; the tests include a puzzle designed to be hard for plain backtracking.
hints: Keep three arrays of 9-bit masks (rows, columns, boxes) so that the digits still allowed in a cell are `~(row | col | box) & 0x1FF`. Counting the bits of that mask tells you which empty cell has the fewest options.

For unique permutations, sort first. When choosing a value for the next position, skip `nums[i]` if it equals `nums[i - 1]` and `nums[i - 1]` is **not** currently used: that ordering was already produced with the earlier copy.
